findings.claim: EPA approved Percepto's Air Max OGI system as an alternative test method for periodic screening, and EPA found it meets the periodic screening requirements for the 1 kg/hr detection threshold.
findings.quote: EPA has determined that Percepto's Air Max OGI System meets the periodic screening requirements for the1 kg/hr detection threshold. (The source PDF reads 'for the1'.)
findings.quote_status: verified in the page images, pages 2 and 3 of the letter
findings.why_it_matters: This is the dated federal movement. It names the detection threshold EPA actually accepted, and EPA's threshold is 1 kg/hr, not the 100 g/hr that the vendor advertises.

findings.claim: After collection, a certified OGI inspector reviews the survey footage to identify emissions, which triggers a follow-up inspection.
findings.quote: Once the data are collected from the Air Max, a certified OGI inspector reviews the collected survey footage to identify any emissions, triggering a follow-up inspection.
findings.quote_status: verified in the page image, page 2
findings.why_it_matters: This is the strongest source answer to the opening question of who decides it is a leak. The approval letter places a certified human in that step, and it does not describe any AI detection step.

findings.claim: The only AI reference in the approval letter is the title of a separate sampling protocol. The software named AIM is an acronym for autonomous inspection and monitoring, not artificial intelligence.
findings.quote: Sampling protocol (alternative test method) titled 'Percepto Autonomous OGI UAS & AI Software Alternative Test Method' (March 26, 2025, updated September 1, 2025). Also: 'Percepto Autonomous Inspection & Monitoring (AIM) cloud-based software to execute flights, and view and retrieve collected data.' MATM-14 section 3.1.1: 'Autonomous Inspection & Monitoring or AIM means the software through which the Site Owner/Operator can interact with the UAS, execute flights, and view and retrieve collected data.'
findings.quote_status: verified in the page images. MATM-14 wording verified in the page images, pages 3 and 4
findings.why_it_matters: This is the single most important false-inference guard. The AI label is a protocol title. The 'AIM' software is not AI. The AI role in detection is not described by the EPA letter and remains unverified.

findings.claim: The approval letter says the pilot is trained to identify emissions, and the approval is not an endorsement of any company or product.
findings.quote: a US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) certified pilot who is also trained to identify potential emissions. / This approval letter is not an implied or express endorsement by EPA of any specific companies or products, as EPA does not promote the products, services, or enterprises of non-federal entities.
findings.quote_status: verified in the page images, pages 1 and 3
findings.why_it_matters: Two human roles are named, the FAA-certified pilot and the certified OGI inspector. The EPA letter does not endorse Percepto, so the story can't present the approval as an endorsement of the vendor's performance.

findings.claim: The EPA method document describes a drone flying a pre-programmed flight plan to points of interest, with a notice that identifies the time in the footage when a leak occurred.
findings.quote: The Air Max OGI UAS is deployed via a ruggedized, weather-proof solution permanently installed in close proximity to the equipment to be surveyed. / If a leak is identified, after the mission is completed, Percepto sends a notification to the Site Owner/Operator that identifies the specific time in the video footage of the mission when the leak occurred.
findings.quote_status: verified in the page images, pages 2 and 3 of the MATM-14 document
findings.why_it_matters: This is the mechanism to picture: a permanent station, a planned route, a footage bookmark and a notice. It is the source for the opening and consequence rows.

findings.claim: The method was submitted by the vendor with a field-verified sensitivity of 0.1 kg/hr at 90 percent probability, under wind speeds up to 20 kph and standoff distances of 20 to 140 feet. This is the method's own claim, not an EPA-verified figure.
findings.quote: This method has a field-verified method sensitivity to reliably detect fugitive methane emissions of 0.1 kg/hr with a 90% probability of detection under a variety of real-world operational conditions, including variable wind speeds up to 20 kph and at standoff detection distances ranging from 20 to 140 feet.
findings.quote_status: verified in the page image, page 1
findings.why_it_matters: This is the method document's own sensitivity claim. It is numerically different from the threshold EPA found met (1 kg/hr), so the story must name which one is which.

filmability.viewer_question: When a drone flags a leak over Permian equipment, who decides it is a leak?
filmability.opening_action: An illustrated drone lifts from a permanently installed weatherproof station beside oilfield equipment and flies a preset route to points of interest. The on-screen label must say illustration.
filmability.mechanism: Per the EPA method, the drone flies a planned route, records infrared video of each point of interest, and bookmarks the footage time at which a leak occurred. A certified OGI inspector then reviews the footage to identify emissions, which triggers a follow-up inspection. The AI role claimed by the vendor is not described in the EPA letter.
filmability.human_consequence: A notice with a timestamp goes to the operator, which triggers a follow-up inspection of the flagged equipment. No source reports a detection count, a repair, an emissions result or an enforcement outcome from any Permian deployment.
filmability.source_limit: The EPA letter approves a periodic screening method. It says EPA does not endorse any company or product. It places a certified human inspector in the review step. The vendor's AI claim is in trade press only. The 0.1 kg/hr performance is the method's own claim. The federal satellite route is paused to January 22, 2027 and proposed to be rescinded, but that proposal is not yet published.

recommended_angle.approach: Explanatory animation for the mechanism, with the EPA letter's sentences as the decisive evidence. No observed footage is sourced. No human subject is sourced.
recommended_angle.why_this_structure: The EPA letter is the one primary document that changes the answer about who checks the footage. A mechanism-led cut would have to invent the plume and the detection, which the sources do not show. A human-led cut has no sourced person, so it would manufacture a feeling.
ordering: Dated decision: EPA approved an Austin company's drone camera method on September 30th, 2025.
Decisive source detail: a certified OGI inspector reviews the footage, and the AI label is a protocol title.
Mechanism: a planned route over points of interest, a 1 kg/hr threshold EPA accepted, and a timestamped notice.
Alternative federal route: third-party satellite and aerial super-emitter notices at 100 kg/hr, paused to January 22, 2027 and proposed to be rescinded.
Unresolved: the proposal is not published, no Permian deployment results are published, and the AI's role is unverified.
recommended_angle.likely_false_inference: That EPA approved AI that finds and fixes leaks, or that EPA is rolling back leak detection.
recommended_angle.prevents_it: The letter's no-endorsement sentence and its human-review sentence, and the March 2026 fact sheet, which changes flare monitoring only.

filmability.counter_image: The Railroad Commission's own drone team, described as emergency response, and the RRC's 2025 opposition letter. Both show what the state regulator does and does not do.
filmability.earned_take: The approved leak check in the Permian can be the operator's own drone with a human reviewer, while the federal third-party satellite route is paused until January 22, 2027 and proposed for rescission. No source shows how many leaks have been found or fixed.
unsupported_spoken_concepts: The AI detects the leak. No source shows an AI detection output or who checks it.
Permian drones have found N leaks. No verified count exists. The 130-event figure in a search summary was not fetched and must not be used.
The Railroad Commission uses drones or AI to find methane. No source supports it.
Most Texas releases are never reported. The cited RMI page does not say it.

EPA is rolling back leak detection. The October 7th release names covers, control device monitoring and marginal wells in its plan, but the text is unpublished, and the release says nothing on leak detection.
filmability.source_limit_detail: The strongest primary-source limitation is that the approval letter places the detection judgment with a certified human inspector and does not describe any AI detection step. The AI claim exists only in vendor and journalism sources. Those sources also say the vendor's own performance numbers are its own. The next limitation is that the rescission is announced but not published.
filmability.county: unresolved. No site or county is named in any source. Midland is the only sourced Permian place name, as the site of Percepto's operational hub (DroneXL), and it is not an emission site. The director must find a sourced site before naming a county.

visual_stakes.opening_question: When a drone flags a leak over Permian equipment, who decides it is a leak?
visual_stakes.answer: Under EPA's approval letter, a certified OGI inspector reviews the footage. The vendor says its AI flags likely leaks. The letter does not describe that AI step, and no source reports how often it is right.
